utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I gather it's been agreed that a witness will be interposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, this is Dr. Antonio Alonso.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please bring in Dr. Alonso.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while he's brought, I'll indicate that he's a DNA expert. He will be testifying in relation to the identification of the bodies found at Batajnica, and particularly relevant to paragraphs 75(d), 77, and Schedule D of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Alonso. Would you please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think both microphones should be in the usual place for the witness and not for the interpreter; and if the second one causes a problem, then I rely on the interpreter to deal with that problem. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Alonso.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please state your name and profession.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: My name is Antonio Alonso, and I am at the National Institute of Toxicology and Forensic Sciences in Madrid, Spain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what is your profession and what do you do there?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I am an expert in genetic identification in the forensic field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And how long have you been working in that field?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I've been working at the biology services for the past 22 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, Your Honours, the CV for Dr. Alonso is P2501 which we wish to tender. It is pretty extensive and it speaks for itself, so we will not go through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Dr. Alonso --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we admit the CV of the Doctor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doctor, did you receive from Dr. Dusan Dunjic of the Belgrade Institute for Forensic Sciences both samples in respect to human remains that were found according to what you were told at a place called Batajnica in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. Our institute received, in the course of 2001, 56 remains of bones for genetic analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you receive from the International Commission for Missing Persons, and also from the ICTY, blood reference samples of family members of persons who were said to have been missing from a place called Suva Reka or killed in a place called Suva Reka in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. My apologies for coughing. We received 13 blood samples from those two organisations that you mentioned, and indeed these were samples from people who were family members of people who disappeared in Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, Doctor, I understand that you performed analyses of the material that you received and provided four reports in respect to the results of those analyses. The last report dated the 13th of June, 2006, I understand is a sort of compendium or a summary of the findings in the previous three reports and also describes application of later technology to the analyses of the samples that you received. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes. It is this last report which is a compendium of all the analyses carried out previously, and it also contains analysis with new DNA markers. I would like to make it very clear at this point that in this analysis, we have used three types of DNA. One DNA, which we give 50 percent, depending on whether it is the father or the mother, and which we pass on to our children and at a 50 percent basis as well. This DNA has been used to prove most of the identifications we conducted, but in addition to that we've used two other types of DNA. One type of DNA that only mothers pass on to their children, and that is called mitochondrial DNA, and therefore is shared by all the siblings, children, produced by that same mother. And then the last form of analysis we conducted is DNA from the I [as interpreted] chromosome passed by males on to their male descendents. Therefore we have used three genetic analysis tools for all the remains where identification or compatibility was involved as per the reference samples they were being compared to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. I see that it says with respect to the last method of analysis that you used DNA from the I chromosome. Is that the I or the Y chromosome?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Y chromosome, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last report, Your Honour, of the 17th of November is P2486 which you can obviously see. Unless necessary, I don't think there's any need to tender the previous two, three, reports; they are summarised in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sir, thank you. P2486 will be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doctor, on the 13th of June this year, did you also provide some responses in writing to some questions that had been submitted to you by the ICTY in respect to your report?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And therein you explained various aspects of the report?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: In the report we were being asked as to what the functions of our institute were, in other words, the place where we conducted the analysis. We responded that the official centre of the Spanish Ministry of Justice for conducting forensic science analysis and toxicology analysis. More specifically, the biology service, where I am employed and where these analyses were conducted, conducts the general functions of assisting the Ministry of Justice and, more specifically, it is the official entity at the Ministry of Justice for forensic genetics. In the report we provide answers to other questions, such as the quality guarantees applicable to the analysis we conduct at the biology service, and the answers in this respect provide the proficiency tests conducted on an annual basis at our centre. And we also speak about our own development of research techniques in this particular field. Now, as to the questions about the methods we used and whether these methods are in keeping with the latest scientific developments, our answer is positive. Yes. We've used state-of-the-art technology, and throughout the world at present there is major standardisation in the DNA analysis methods that we use in forensics. So a method used by our laboratory is a method that can be reproduced at a second analysis conducted by any other centre, and that's a very important type of guarantee in this field. Another thing we were being asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you continue. I'm sorry to interrupt you, but just to facilitate the Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just indicate that that is P2487.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you continue with your explanation, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Other questions that we were being asked were whether the results of the statistic valuation of analysis could vary significantly on the basis of different populations; more specifically, if it were an Albanian population. There's many theoretical answers that can be provided to this question, but the most adequate answer is the one we provided, which is to re-calculate the analysis results on the basis of an Albanian population using a study that was published in the Forensic Science International magazine. And we saw that the results did not vary significantly. They are very similar, and they are within the values that can be expected within the father-son, mother-son, or father-mother-son parameters that we've previously seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. That --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The response, as I indicated is P2487, which we also ask be received in evidence as an addendum to the main report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. That will be received in evidence, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could have a look at the report, Doctor, of the 17th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is P2486, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many positive findings of identification did you make in respect to the material that you received and analysed.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes. There is a total of 21 identifications, 19 of which are on the basis of DNA analysis, with 50 percent; and 50 [as interpreted] regions of this DNA which provide 50 percent and which are based on a father-son, mother-son, or a father-mother-son type of relationship. 19 of these identifications out of 21 are given in the report as scientifically proven. And there are two of these identifications, however, which are based on the analyse of mitochondrial and chromosome Y analysis, which have a lower discriminating ability, and we thus call these identifications preliminary identifications. Therefore, 19 identifications are proven and two identifications are of a preliminary nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I think there's a make in the transcript at line 18 on page 6, and I have a feeling that should be 15 regions rather than 50. Doctor, you've been interpreting as saying that 19 of these were on the basis of DNA analysis with 50 percent and 50 regions of this DNA. Now, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, these are based on 15 DNA regions, each of which are inherited 50 percent from one or the other parent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doctor, we don't have time to go through all the results. I'd like to go through a couple of them with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The results, Your Honour, are in the English translation of this report at page 4, and it's really under the heading "Results."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You used the term in respect to these results that you cannot rule out the possibility that the bone sample Ba-32 comes from Berisha Nebi, Sofije, the biological mother of Kuqui (Vesel) Dashurije. You also tell us in your previous answer that you regard the identifications as proven. In that context, can you explain the expression, "cannot rule out the possibility."

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: In each of these 19 cases, after conducting a reference of the reference samples and analysing the genetic profile of the bone remains, and after conducting a blind analysis of one against all the others, initially - because of course at the beginning we don't know which sample belongs to whom - after all that we obtain a series of compatibility. Now, as per your question, sir, the answer is that 50 percent of those bone remains in the Ba-32 sample are under reference number 5. That means we cannot exclude the women from which these remains come from, that is to say the mother, reference number 5. What is the degree of probability with which we can make such a statement? Well, what we do is assess how many more times how more probable this observed genetic compatibility is in the two regions and between these two samples if we consider that the parental relationship, paternity in this case, is maybe not this relationship; in other words, any other mother within that same population. So when we conduct this calculation, we obtain what we call the likelihood index or the likelihood ratio, in English, and that is a figure which tells us how reliable our results are. Now, if it's easier for the Tribunal to understand the probability data in terms of percentages, I could then say that a LR of 1.000 is equivalent to 99.9 percent. A likelihood ratio of a 10.000 would be the equivalent of 99.99 percent. 100.000 would be 99.999 percent. That is to say that all of the results are above 99.9 percent likelihood, and I would add that these calculations are conducted only with that DNA which is provided on a 50 percent basis. We have not included here subsequent checking of all the cases with DNA from mitochondrial or chromosome Y DNA with different markers, as I said before. But in any case we have verified that when we have a mother and their daughter they have the same mitochondrial DNA. And when we have a father bone among the reference samples and a son among the reference samples, they also share the same Y chromosome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to look at just two others of the results. If you look at page 5 of the report, the last two results on that page in which you speak of Redon Nexhat. Before I have the question may I ask something. Generally speaking, in your report, you use the surname first, followed by the father's name in brackets, and followed by the given name of the person whom you refer.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: In most of the cases, we have used that format for names; however, not always. In the samples we received, we noticed that this particular format for the name was not always used. In other words, father's surname, then name, and so forth. In some occasions the reference samples we received contained the individual's first name and then the family name. And that is why sometimes, since we're not familiar with the surnames or with the order in which they should be provided, what we did is transcribe the information as we received it. So that is why I think regarding your question in some cases we have name and surname of the father -- name of the father, but sometimes we're missing the surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. So in respect to the penultimate result on page 5, I'll just read the findings: "So we cannot rule out the possibility that Ba-46 could come from Redon Nexhat, Shyhrete Berisha's biological son." Can you comment on that in respect to what you just said. Let me put this way. Having come to the Tribunal, yesterday, did you have a look again at the family tree; and having done so, could you -- would you like to make any correction in respect to the finding in respect to Redon Nexhat.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Not as regards to identification, nor the data obtained. We obtained compatibility between these remains in comparison to the Shyhrete Berisha data. So Ba-46 can be considered to come from someone who can be considered as the biological son of Shyhrete Berisha. And that is the reference that we have called BS, B as in boy and S as in sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You received for the purpose of your analysis a family tree in respect to the blood reference samples that you were given?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That, Your Honour, is P2500. Could that be put on the ELMO, please -- sorry, the e-court, could we call it up on the e-court, P2500. And if we go to the next page. The next one, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see the family tree there. You see to the right of the family tree in the second -- let's say the second row you see Nexhat and Shyhrete as a couple. And you see below them, Majlinda, daughter; Herolinda, daughter, Altin, son; Redon, son. Please say, "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having regard to that, if we look again at the report in respect to your finding at 75, would you agree with me that Nexhat in respect to the finding for Redon and Majlinda and Herolinda refer to the father of these persons?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: We have not obtained any samples, both samples, for males that are compatible with this individual; however, we consider on the basis of the information that he is the father.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm -- certainly did not understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can -- the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On your family tree, Redon is -- he's not represented -- I see, he's not son -- there's a missing line, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There's a line -- there ought to be a line from Nexhat-Shyhrete, as a couple, to the children, but it's based on the family tree. The four persons below those persons are the children of Nexhat and Shyhrete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And one of them is Redon?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One of them is Redon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that the person who is identified in the paragraph you've been looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what the paragraph says. What's incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The paragraph does not identify him as Redon Berisha, as in the other findings where it gives the surname, followed by the father's name in brackets, followed by the first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it should be Redon Nexhat Berisha?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it should be Berisha Nexhat Redon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To clarify further, Your Honours, if I may. The same would apply to the last paragraph of that page, the other two siblings, Majlinda and Herolinda are referred to. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I have nothing further in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Doctor, I have one question. The two identifications that were of a preliminary nature, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From our standpoint, since these identifications are based on DNA regions that allow us to obtain information on the maternal or paternal lines of descendents, the discrimination power that they have is not equal to that of the other markers. In other terms, at present it is very easy to prove a father-son or mother-son relationship through markings that are provided on a 50 percent basis. But it is more difficult to prove that two people are siblings and share the same father or same mother. And that's what we have here. We have a reference sample, and we have a bone remains sample, which are compatible in terms of siblings on the basis of chromosome Y and mitochondrial analysis. However, statistically, this does not have a definitive value, and it is called preliminary proof. There is compatibility on the maternal line. There is compatibility on the paternal line, but we need to take into account that most of the people who disappeared are members of the same family. If you look at the appendices in the end and look at the Y chromosome we've obtained, you will see there are very few compared to what one might expect in unrelated population. And these two mean that the value of these markers is lower when conducting a statistical assessment of this compatibility between the population. All of this, according to the standards of identification in the forensic field, point at the fact that these samples supposedly belong to these same individuals, but new reference samples would be necessary to be able to confirm that. What samples? Well, we would need the father's or the son's, because then we could analyse this other DNA which would give us the higher discrimination ability. I hope I've answered your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Doctor, on the basis of the restricted information you have in these two cases, are you able to give a likelihood ratio for identification of the two persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If one looks or assesses these DNA profiles on a database containing Y chromosome and mitochondrial information, we would be at a likelihood ratio located between 100 and 1.000, 100 and 1.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And tell me how that converts to percentage likelihood terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have a value of 100, we're talking about 99.0 percentage; and if we have 1.000, we're talking about 99.9. I would again state that from our standpoint these two identifications should not be considered as proven until new analysis are conducted. From our standpoint, there is no certainty because the possibility of their existing another individual in the population unrelated to the person we're now analysing is relatively high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will be my lack of understanding, Doctor, but I'm not following this part of it. You've given us an indication that the likelihood of identification in the other 19 cases is at least 99.9 percent. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the other cases, the level is at least above 99.9 percent in all of the cases. And in many cases the number of 9s after the comma is even higher, which gives us even higher certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the two we are discussing at the moment, are you saying there is a 99 percent likelihood that they are the persons referred to, and that there's only a 1 percent possibility that they are not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But even if the figures are such and appear to give certainty, we know that they do not give full certainty. And that is why generally it is preferred to present data by referring to a hypothesis where maybe it is not the person. Let me help you understand. All of the members of the family --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. No, carry on. I was going to say something else. I'll say it when you're finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of the members of a same family, all siblings, all uncles, or aunts who share the same maternal line share the same mitochondrial DNA, which is what we've used in these last two cases. Therefore, we cannot differentiate amongst them; they are the same. In other words, this DNA allows for the differentiation of family lines rather than individuals, and this is where the limitation lies. There is less variability as to these types of DNA, and that is why its discrimination power or ability is lower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But in this case, the DNA you're using is from bone fragments. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's rather different from blood which may pass -- even though a person has not died, we've got a fragment of bone which makes at least makes it clear we've got a deceased body; and we would then be able to look at other evidence pointing to the circumstances in which certain people may have died, which we can take along with your analysis and perhaps come to a more definitive conclusion than you're able to do scientifically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably other data arising from the investigation can help to increase or decrease the uncertainty around these two cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How does the family tree become established in the course of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Become established, you mean what's the basis of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, the relationships. Are these --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there evidence already of all these relationships?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The family tree here that was sent was something that was compiled by ICTY investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness, Shyhrete Berisha, provided a family tree in evidence, which I think is substantial, at least to the extent it is relevant substantial to the evidence that is provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we now have all the evidence to establish the relationships, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. And in respect to the -- what he described as preliminary findings, the additional samples were analysed by another DNA facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that evidence is yet to come?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, of these 21 victims, how many are specified in a schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 15 of them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is Schedule D?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Schedule D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what is to happen with the others that have now been identified, but don't appear in the schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Prosecution -- the Prosecution is considering and indeed intends to make an appropriate application in respect to correlating the evidence and the schedules, which we hope to do when some more of the evidence is in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will proceed in the follow order: General Lukic, General Lazarevic, General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Sainovic, and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Alonso. My name is Branko Lukic. I appear on behalf of General Sreten Lukic before this Tribunal. I have a few questions only, and I believe we can wrap up in ten to 15 minutes. If, during my cross-examination, you wish to consult your notes, please feel free to whenever you deem it necessary. My cross-examination will not deal itself with the essence, the gist, of your findings; rather, what I will try to gain from you is the data on the dynamics of the work done, since during this trial there were some issues that were discussed which you may not have touched upon. May we begin? Your biology department of the Institute of Toxicology in Madrid and yourself were tasked to conduct a DNA analysis in order to identify human remains, that is bones, for which it was presumed belonged to 56 different bodies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Maybe the number of bodies was not 56 but 59. 56 is what we received, but in any case I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was it who estimated that these remains belonged to 56 or 59 bodies?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: We had 56 sets of remains that had been previously analysed by anthropological means. When we conducted our own analysis of these remains, what we saw was that there were only 41 genetic profiles. As the discrimination power of these analyses is high, we can consider that among these remains there were only 41 people represented and, more specifically, there were ten people who had double samples and two people who presented triplicate samples. That's the data that I can provide by way of an answer. Now, as to the supposition of the total number of victims, that is not a figure that we provide. It is the person conducting the investigation, in this case the General Medicine Institute of Belgrade. And I suppose, and I repeat in supposition, they came to this figure on the basis of the number of people who had disappeared, and that's how they came up with 59 victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know whether, in Batajnica, whole bodies were found or just pieces or parts of bodies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: That is right. I did not know. We received samples from a diathesis of a long bone for each of those samples. That's all we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Dr. Dusan Dunjic, who is the director for the Forensic Medicine in Belgrade, transported those bones to your institute. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when Professor Dunjic brought those remains to your institute?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I believe I recall, but let me confirm that it was 22nd of November of 2001. Let me check. Just a second, please. I don't have the date available to me here, but I think it was 22 November 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the remains brought by Professor Dunjic, were they properly packaged? Were they properly preserved in that sense?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes. As I said to you before, these were sections from the diathesis of the long bone. Each of the bones was in a container, in a hermetically sealed jar and each of them contained a single and distinct identification label.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we may conclude that the cooperation you received on the part of Dr. Dunjic was at a professional level?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your preliminary report was drafted on the 15th of November, 2002 [as interpreted]. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you send that preliminary report to The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: On the date that you said is the date when the report was mailed, both to Professor Dunjic and to The Hague Tribunal on the 15th of February, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And an identification process is a long and complicated one. Would you agree with me, if I said that?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only for the transcript, Your Honour, I can see that on the page 19 line 5, it was either misspoken by me or wrongly entered. It should be 15th of February, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has clarified it already. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Alonso, the preliminary report dated 15th of February, isn't the only report you drafted concerning this issue. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: No. It's not the only report. It's the first report concerning this group of samples.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your additional reports were submitted on the 4th of July, 2004; on the 10th of December, 2002; and the 17th of November, 2004?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The first date should have been 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which also shows that it was a long and complicated process?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes. Due to the complexity arising from the number of individuals and to the fact that they were related; that's what provided the greatest complexity from a technical standpoint as regards the analysis that we needed to conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking all this was because of the following question. Is it correct that the repatriation of the bodies, that is the handing over of the bodies to their families, could have only been done after the identification performed by you?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I suppose so, but I cannot say. I cannot say whether there are other samples from these same bodies being analysed in other laboratories. I don't know what other types of analysis, in addition to the ones that were requested from our own genetic analysis centre, are being requested or conducted, either topological analysis or other types analysis. So I'm afraid I cannot respond reliably to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Doctor, were you ever asked to have regard to the need to repatriate the bodies in prioritising your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, at no moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be correct if I said the Belgrade experts had an additional task when identifying bodies by using your results. This was another long procedure?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I do not know the use to which our report results were put to -- by our colleagues in Belgrade. As regards the identification of the bodies, as I said, I don't know what the condition of the bodies was, whether they were full, complete bodies and had been submitted to anthropological analysis, I know nothing of all of these aspects, sir. All I can tell you is about the analysis we conducted scientifically on small bone samples that we received from these alleged victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. This exhausts my questions, and I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said about other analyses might have been done by other institutions. Do you know if the ICMP did any analysis with respect to DNA samples from human remains?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I do not know; however, in our last report we requested of the Tribunal that in the appendix containing the results of the DNA analysis provided in this lab report, we asked, if possible, for ICMP to be informed, because just as we identified 19 people plus two with a lesser probability, there's other remains that continue to remain anonymous. And if they were cross-checked against the International Commission for Missing Persons database, that might allow for establishment of coincidental compatibility providing for a greater number of identifications. But I do not know whether other analyses have been conducted on these remains. I think that would be positive for the process, and I think it would be good for the people concerned for these profiles to be cross-checked with the family databases that ICMP has.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dr. Alonso, that completes your evidence; thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you've now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We now have to break so that the arrangements for the continued evidence of Mr. Tanic can be put in place. That will be a 20-minute break until 10.20. Unless I hear to the contrary that this is not convenient for parties and, in particular, the interpreters, we would then sit from 10.20 to 11.50 and from 12.20 till 1.45. So we will resume at 10.20 and we will resume in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Tanic. The delay this resuming your evidence was caused by interposing another witness, and it was convenient to everyone and to the Court to do that. So I'm sorry you've been further inconvenienced, but hopefully we'll manage to get to the end of your evidence now quite quickly. The cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman will continue, and, as before, the solemn declaration continues to apply to your evidence. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I should tell you that in accordance with -- with our not particularly satisfactory conversation at the end of yesterday's session, at least I felt I may have gone a little overboard with you. I'm sorry about that. But I have dramatically cut back the questions I'm going to ask today and without I think interfering with the things I want to do. That happens when you have time for preparation that you can reflect on what you want to ask and take the time to be better prepared and therefore move more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Bench is grateful for that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I'm now going to refer to paragraph 98 of your statement. You speak about information on the commission of crimes by the UCK, and you say: "In the autumn of 1999, one Western country asked me to assist in handling this information -- in handing this information and evidence over to the ICTY through unofficial channels." What western country was it that asked you to do that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: United Kingdom, and this refers to crimes against the Serbs, particularly those committed by the Haradinaj brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And who was it you spoke to from the United Kingdom that asked you to do this, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A high representative of the British intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I assume that's a name that you really aren't permitted to divulge?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm prepared to respect that. Did you hand such information over to the ICTY before you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never arrested. I was kidnapped and tortured. This information I forwarded to the SDB. They started to collect documentation on the crimes committed by Agim Ceku and the Haradinaj brothers. After that the kidnapping of me and wife, the torture occurred; and after that, I discontinued work on that. Work on that was continued through Mr. Mijatovic, and he delivered that material to the ICTY after the year 2000. We're referring to crimes against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the answer is you didn't deliver any information to the ICTY, as a result of that request?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the crimes against the Serbs, that information, or the information they requested for the material on the crimes to be prepared?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm only talking about the information you talked about when you said a western country asked you to turn information over to the ICTY. The answer is you didn't turn any over as a result of that request, you personally? I think that's your answer. If you can just say "yes," we can go on.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, this is an unfair question. The foreign service asked from our service to prepare material on the crimes against the Serbs to be forwarded to the ICTY. And the information about that I forwarded to the ICTY before being kidnapped, just information, not the materials because I had not received them. And our SDB was in the process of collecting the material and information about that and were later handed over to the ICTY; not through me, but through Mr. Zoran Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what -- what are the unofficial channels that you can hand information to the ICTY, as opposed to official channels, what would be the unofficial channels that you speak of?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you wait for me to read this paragraph out because there seems to be a bit of confusion regarding the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a sentence that starts with the words: "In the autumn of 1999, one Western country ..."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it. Thank you. Yes. Thank you. I don't know which channels they would use to hand the material over to the ICTY, so I don't know what are these unofficial channels. The point here is is that it was requested from our security service to prepare these materials. This was requested from me by that foreign country so that they could forward it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've answered the question, but let me -- let me suggest to you "unofficial channels" were your words, not mine. So what did you mean when you said, "unofficial channels of the ICTY"? Just tell us what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think he said unofficial channels of the ICTY. He's referring to unofficial channels of Serbia to give the material to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful for Mr. Hannis helping me with the possible answer, but that isn't what he said. It can be interpreted that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It can be interpreted in various ways, so please carry on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What did you mean by "unofficial channels"?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Maybe it would be easier for Mr. Tanic to have a copy in English because of different references; 166, 167, et cetera. Maybe this would facilitate translation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will speed up matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's not a matter that I can interfere in through your good offices, Mr. Fila. It's Mr. Ackerman who's conducting this cross-examination, and it's for him to decide what's the best way to do it. And I would be surprised if English -- an English copy was really what was best in these circumstances, since the witness -- well, perhaps it was only an English copy that was signed, was it? Mr. Ackerman, was it only an English copy that was signed initially?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he gave his original statement in English. His statement was given in English, so it might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Anything that would speed up his answers would be helpful. I thought I had made some progress. I thought I had made process in trying to move rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: See if you can give us an answer just as briefly as possible about what you meant when you used the words "unofficial channels."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unofficial channels would be personal contacts, because Milosevic's regime did not want to cooperate officially with the ICTY, not even when it concerned Serbian victims. But which personal contacts those would be, I don't know. But I know that unofficial channels would be personal contacts. It was explained later in this sentence, "since Milosevic was not willing to hand it over officially."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've answered the question, I appreciate it. When I -- just a moment ago, in one of my questions, I asked if you handed this information over before you were arrested, and you quarrelled with that. And said you were not arrested, but you were kidnapped. If you look at the last sentence of that paragraph, 98, talking about information you were collecting for your book and so forth, you said this in your statement: "I was accused of collecting this information because I'm a spy for Western countries." So the people that arrested you suspected you of being a spy, and you were arrested on suspicion of being a spy. That's not a kidnapping, it's an arrest. And it's a perfectly valid arrest if they had information, and they did, that you were giving information to foreign sources. And when they said to you, you were being arrested because of suspicion of being a spy, it was an arrest, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I object, Your Honour. There's nothing -- I haven't seen the foundation for where they said they were arresting him for being a spy. Can we have a citation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The last sentence of paragraph 98, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I read that, but I don't see that that supports your question the way it was phrased. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the alternative is that it's an admission he was a spy. You can have it either way. I'll take it either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is admissible in my view. Mr. Tanic, would you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say I was officially charged. They accused me during beating me that -- and accused me of being a spy for western powers. But collection of information about Serb victims of crimes in Kosovo can hardly be called a spying for western country. Had I really been a spy, I would have been charged, indicted, but no indictment was issued. And don't be surprised one day that different intelligence services that cooperate among themselves and including our intelligence service cooperated through me. Mr. Ackerman, I was never arrested, I was never indicted for espionage, I was never convicted, I was never a spy. I performed intelligence dimension matters of political problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I put this to you: In your quest for asylum status, if you had said, I was arrested for being a spy, you wouldn't have been able to gain asylum. You had to say, I was kidnapped and beaten, and there's a threat against my life; and, therefore, I'm seeking asylum. And that's in fact what happened; you made that up to get asylum, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did occur. I was kidnapped. I was beaten up, together with my wife. That was probably an attempted murder, and this was confirmed in the book, quoted by your Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to go on to something else now. In paragraph 113 of your statement, you talk about a statement -- you talk about Milosevic issuing orders that the army basically hide from NATO to avoid casualties. Do you remember that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 113, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think that information begins -- let me find it. It's paragraph 110: "Under Milosevic's orders, the army's main strategy was to hide from NATO attacks." And I want to ask you about your statement then in paragraph 113, where you say: "As soon as NATO saw troop movements on the ground, they were sure to target." How is it, if you know, NATO would see troop movements on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very easily through technical means, through reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to go to paragraph 116 now and 117. And you've already talked about these things and I just have a very brief question to ask you. You talked about getting information from western sources that Zastava, which is a military and car factory, would be targeted by NATO and that the RTS building would be targeted by NATO. And I have just, like, maybe two questions about that. First of all, this information was information that you received actually during the bombing, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you say that you personally, paragraph 117: "I personally passed on to Milosevic information I'd received from my Western contacts that RTS was a target." Where was that you personally passed that on to him? Where were you, where was he?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot name those sources. I cannot divulge them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about any sources. That's apparently a translation problem. What I asked you was: When you personally told Milosevic about this, where were you and where was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he says he personally passed it on, that may not mean the same thing as told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if Mr. Hannis could avoid assisting the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Hannis, I don't think that was a really very helpful intervention in the circumstances. This is a cross-examination where particular points can be put directly to the witness, and there's nothing wrong with the question that's being asked there. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask it again. When you say you personally told Milosevic about this, my question is: Where were you and where was he?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I personally relayed this information, not handed it over. Transfer of information was done through communication means of the SDB. It says I transferred and not handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know, do you, that this was actually transferred, that Milosevic actually received this information?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And there was information from other sources. I wasn't the sole source of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And because of your vast experience in the intelligence business, you know, don't you, that one of the most closely held and closely guarded secrets are targeting information during bombing. That information is not even given to pilots until briefings right before take-off. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, Mr. Ackerman. During NATO bombing, a certain leak of information was permitted for the reason to leave some rule for an honourable way out. There was some other considerations, but I cannot now dwell on intelligence procedures, state secrets of certain countries. It's too much of a burden for me. I can tell you that Mr. Milosevic had information on targets, and you may invite Serbia's intelligence service representatives to provide you documentation. On that, I was one of the sources; I wasn't the sole source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, at the beginning of that paragraph, 117, the phrase used is: "I personally passed on to Milosevic information that I had received." What do you mean "personally passed on to Milosevic?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean that I personally was the source, and I passed it on through the previously established communication means that were known to be leading to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what you in fact did was pass information to the SDB. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the SDB controlled those means of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we had some evidence about this when Mr. Fila was cross-examining you, but I certainly until now would have read that as if you had a personal, direct contact with Milosevic over this. That's how it reads. And it's helpful to have it clarified. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, be careful how you answer this question; think carefully. Do you know if General Clark or General Short knew that targeting information was being passed to you and then to the Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, I have no idea what General Clark knew at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about General Short, do you think General Short knew this information was being passed to you and through you to the Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, absolutely. How could I know what they knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So since you don't know that, then I need you to tell me who passed this information to you.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you trying to drive a wedge between me and the west? This source is fully protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. I'm trying to represent my client and to test your credibility. And one of the ways we test your credibility is for you to tell us who told you something that you claim you heard so that we can ask that person if you're telling the truth. So tell me who told you this.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that, absolutely cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think under Rule 90 that you have the power to compel him to answer and I ask you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if you do, I ask that you consider that being done in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To which I would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would, though, Mr. Hannis, welcome some more guidance on this. I think this particular matter is one where the witness has also declined to identify the person in the SDB to whom he gave the information. I think in the cross-examination by Mr. Fila, he said it was done through an arranged means of communication by code, but wouldn't say to whom it was given. And so we have an absence of identification of both where the information came from and how it was relayed to its destination. Now, in view of the sensitivity of this matter, to continue this debate, we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, in the transcript of your transcript from the 10th of November at page 6300, you were talking about that meeting in New York and the document that resulted therefrom. And you were asked about the signatures on that document, and you answered this: "There were no signatures, no documents, because, as I said, the negotiations were discreet." Now, isn't it the truth with regard to that document that it bears no signatures because there was no agreement at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was reached on the things specified. I don't know why there are no signatures, though. There may be another piece of paper with the signatures, but you should ask the state department that. As I said, I wasn't in New York, but I was familiar with the preparations of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think what you told us, or at least what I understood from what you told us, that there were no signatures on the document because it was a discreet meeting. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a complicated stop-and-go negotiating procedure. Various means were used; meetings, round-tables, private meetings. There was a lot of change of position, testing the other side, as there always is in such situations. Second of all, there was a grave problem of whether Mihajlovic was to go there with full Milosevic's authority or not. There was some controversial information on that. Agani was there as well. He kept changing his position as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you've answered my question --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very complicated issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- as well as you can. You're going on to a bunch of stuff I didn't ask. You must know, as an international diplomat and negotiator, that discreet secret agreements are signed all the time and kept secret. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is often so, not always though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's good enough. That's good enough. Now, all of these negotiations that you claim to have been having with the Albanian representatives were called by you discreet negotiations. These were secret negotiations, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially they were public, partially semi-secret, partially secret. We used various negotiating means and ways, but we tried to keep it discreet, and yet some leaks were allowed. Sometimes we would have a public round-table; but then during the breaks, there would be meetings which were negotiating in the very narrow sense. Therefore, it would have been done within a public forum, but as to what would happen subsequently was not. Otherwise, I was never an international diplomat. I never called myself that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to another issue. At page 6304 and 6305 of your testimony on the 10th of November, you're talking about the time-period between 1997 and 1998. And you're talking about the KLA, and what you said was this: "At the time the Albanians didn't have a KLA. They weren't organised. They existed mostly abroad; however, at that point Milosevic decided to give up on the political process and started provoking incidents and conflicts in Kosovo together with his associates." Now, first, I'd like you to have a look at an exhibit, P705, and I want to look at page 3 of that exhibit. And there is a box on page 3 of that exhibit that we should be able to find. And not reading Serbian, I'm not sure if it's on the screen or not. But there is a box where you're quoted as saying this, and this article is dated 31 January 1997, very early in 1997. You're quoted as saying this: "The Albanians must themselves find a way to stop terrorist actions in Kosovo in order to contribute towards the trust-building process." Now, if what you said is correct, that at that time the Albanians didn't have a KLA, who was it that was carrying out these terrorist actions in Kosovo that you talk about in January of 1997?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the 10th of November, when was that stated? What year? When did I say that? Here or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 6305 in your testimony here on the 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been a wrong use of words. There were terrorists, but the KLA was not organised as it was at a later stage. There were terrorist activities at first carried out by some local terrorists with the odd member of the KLA here and there. But this is not true for 1997. If I said that, then I must have misspoken. In any case I wanted to say that the KLA was not organised as it became at a later stage. There were some terrorist activities by KLA members in 1997, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... But after telling us that they weren't. Let's look at page 6329, this question: "All right. Let me move on to another topic. In 1997/1998, did you become aware of any international offers to Serbia to help deal with the problem of Albanian terrorist or the UCK? First of all, yes or no." You said: "Yes, but before 1997," therefore in this period but before 1997 as well. Now, you tell us there wasn't any KLA there in 1997 and 1998; and then you say there were offers to deal with the UCK before 1997. How can that be?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I misspoke when interpreting this. Albanian terrorists, there have always been Albanian terrorists down there in Kosovo. But in 1997 they were not as highly organised as they were after Milosevic started provoking incidents and when he gave them political legitimacy. But there were terrorist activities far before that, as early as 1994, 1995. We wanted to negotiate seriously, and we wanted to ask the Albanian side to get rid of terrorists. Rugova and Agani were not happy for having terrorists. At first the KLA was a weakling. It was no match for the Serbian police, special forces, or the military. Perhaps I didn't put it in the best wording, but everyone knows that there was terrorism there. The KLA, in early 1997, was poorly organised, and the Serbian police could have dealt with them with no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... And what you call misspeaking, I call dancing around the truth, as we talked about yesterday. And I suggest, again, that you just make up answers because you think they sound good. Now I'm going on to another subject here. You're talking --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I name the people, the diplomatic representatives of the west, or rather, their countries through which we received the offer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I haven't asked you that.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement in 1998. You're speaking about that at page 6320 of your testimony on 10 November. You say this: "But yes, the agreement with Holbrooke is almost identical to the spirit of these agreements. Holbrooke was naturally familiar with the ways negotiations were going. We had, naturally, contact with the American ambassador. When I say 'we,' I mean Mihajlovic, myself. We also had contact with state department representatives." Now, when did these contacts occur? We're talking about the time of the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the while during the negotiations in 1994, 1995 -- no, 1995, 1996, 1997, all the time we had contact with the American charge d'affaire who was there standing in for the ambassador and with the state department representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. No, you're not listening to my question. You know that I'm not talking about 1994 and 1995. I'm talking about the time of the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement in 1998. And what I want you to tell me is who was the American ambassador that you had contact with at that time, who? Tell me the ambassador's name.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clearly stated here that Holbrooke was familiar with the way the negotiations were being conducted and that we had contact. There is no mention of 1998, although we did have contact in 1998. But at that stage, we were no longer involved in the negotiating process. I clearly stated that I was there from 1994/1995 until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, stop. Your words were put to you: "We had, naturally, contact with the American ambassador." Tell us who that ambassador was. Simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to recall, since it escapes me for the moment. I know I spoke to Chris Hill's brother, who was charge d'affaire of the American embassy at the time. Well, I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This was testimony you gave, what, four or five days ago and now you don't know who it was you were talking about, when you said you had contact with the American ambassador?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forgot what the man's name is. I didn't mention him four or five days ago either. It is not in my memory anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This was the American ambassador to what? Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the American charge d'affaire, since the US lowered its diplomatic -- the level of its diplomatic presence. But he stood in as ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you understand that you used the word "American ambassador." Now, this was the charge d'affaire in Belgrade; is that who you're talking about, the American?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But he performed the role of ambassador; however, he was a charge d'affaire. It is a standard diplomatic manoeuvre --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear that it was the charge d'affaire in Belgrade that you're referring to when you talk about contacts with the American ambassador. That's who it was that you claim to have contact with during the time of the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement. Now, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not clear that it's necessarily during that time. He said they -- Holbrooke was naturally familiar with the way negotiations were going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand the point you're making, Mr. Hannis. I think that's right, Mr. Ackerman, without going into more detail. You can't say it's necessarily at the same time, unless you pin-point the negotiations to the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, line 10 on page 6320 is talking about the agreement with Holbrooke. It's the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but it's his negotiations -- you've got to tie-in his negotiations to be sure we're talking about the same time-scale, and it's not clear in my mind that that is so. It may well be, but it is not clear in my mind that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go on, Your Honour, because I've got enough to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 6315 on 10 November, you were asked this question, and this has to do with the Milosevic statement about less than one million Albanians in Kosovo. The question was: "Let me ask you if you can explain for us a little bit about the significance of that. What difference does it make whether there were one million or one million and a half or 800.000? Why was that important?" Your answer was this: "Well, let me first say that I couldn't understand that either initially; and then I was provided with some explanations, according to which, if they represent less than 10 percent, they can't be considered as a constituent people who would have the right to substantial autonomy." Now, when you say you were provided with some explanations about that, who was it that provided you with those explanations?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several associates of Milosevic's; Ratko Markovic, among others. I discussed this with Stambuk as well. I think that one from Seselj's party mentioned that, and suddenly this figure started appearing. I was confused by the matter whether they were this figure or that. I believe that somebody from the Seselj's party took part in a radio panel or debate, manager of his party in the Belgrade area. But let Seselj decide. Ratko Markovic was the person with whom I discussed this matter. I asked him about that. He didn't -- I cannot say that he explained at a level of a doctrine; he tried to explain it. I'm not sure whether he was certain of that either. Mihajlovic also mentioned that to me. They were trying to use that contacts around Milosevic to lower the number of Albanians to reduce their requests and demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... My only question was who you got the explanations from. Did anybody explain it to you as if it was the law? Did a lawyer tell you, Yes, yes, that's correct, that's the law, or did you not have that kind of an explanation? And just say "yes" or "no." We don't need to have another speech I don't think.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not receive such an explanation by law, on the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. The -- the party that you belonged to, that you told us had six or seven seats in the Assembly and was part of the government, there came a time in 1997 when there were new elections, didn't there?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And after those 1997 elections, how many seats did your party have?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left the government that -- I don't remember the number of seats. We were not part of the single-ballot ticket with them, and this is the option that we took to leave the government. There were several elections around that time; I'm not sure which you refer to. I know that in the latter part of 1997/beginning of 1998, we had distanced from Milosevic's policies for reasons that I'd already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question just -- you were, you know, a major mover in this party. You were -- you said you were a big star. Doesn't the big star know how many seats you had in 1997 -- in 1997?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounds as though we need to know the date of the election you're referring to, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. 23 September 1997, 28 September 1997 -- 28 September 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These were the elections for the Republic Assembly. How many seats did your party gain as a result of those elections?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really absolutely do not remember that. Maybe we had no seats. Really, I did not follow what was going on in the Assembly. I was part of the office of the chairman, of the president. I was dealing with Kosovo, with doctrinary matters. I was never an MP. I never was interested in internal party affairs of that character. This was within the purview of other people, and I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, your guess is consistent with my information, that you had no seats. And what you've told this Court about leaving the government was you left the government because you were persuaded that Milosevic was not accepting a political solution, even though you were presenting one and you were disgusted and so you left the coalition. You actually left the coalition because you had no seats in the government [as interpreted] anymore and you couldn't be in the coalition. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is completely incorrect. We decided not to run on a joint ticket with SPS, JUL, and New Democracy, as before, and since we had decided not to join the joint ticket, which means -- that means we had abandoned the ruling coalition and by doing that we abandoned the government and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours. I'm sorry, John. The transcript intervention, it's 51, 8, it says "seats in the government," actually the question was seats in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go on to your testimony in the Milosevic case page 5171, line 23, a question by Judge May. What was -- and there had apparently just been a video-clip played in court. "What was said on that clip, Mr. Tanic, so that you can deal with this. What was said was that you were not a participant, you were a mere observer, like anybody else in Serbia. What is your answer to that?" Your answer is this: "That is absolutely untrue, and I will later submit documents showing that it's not true. I can also provide at least ten names of domestic figures and international figures who can confirm that I did take part in that." My only question is: Since the 21st of May, 2003 [sic], have you submitted these documents and the names of these persons to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OTP did not request that. They may submit it whenever they wish, because it transpires that this was incorrect. The OTP had press articles that would testify that I was not just a mere observer. If you need additional documents, I can do it but not during this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you've answered my question. And let me ask you another question now. Since you didn't submit those documents that you told you'd submit to the OTP, did you submit any documents to Judge May? Because you said: "I will submit documents." So did you, to Judge May?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm getting no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English translation has disappeared.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have a translation now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, the question I asked you was very simple: Did you submit documents to Judge May, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two photographs were handed over to Judge May; one with Milutinovic, one with Milosevic. They were my photographs, and nobody else requested to do -- me to do anything. I will hand over such documents if requested; no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all right. That's all I wanted to know. Now, when you were having your initial meetings with the Office of the Prosecutor, I want to refer to your testimony about that and specifically to the presence of one or more agents of the British secret service who may have been there. And I think we've now established that it was just one. And in that testimony - and it was page 46 in the draft transcript, I don't have the number of the final transcript - you said this: "A person from the British security service was there for several reasons: First, to verify my identity and then at meetings regarding protection." Now, what kind of meetings were you having regarding protection back when you were giving your statement to the OTP on 21 June 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it wasn't the OTP, but the investigation department of The Hague Tribunal, which is probably part of the OTP; and secondly, such meetings always have security considerations. You never know what can be seen, heard, whether the interpreter is reliable or not - and no offence meant to the interpreters here. Such meetings are always tricky from the security standpoint, as has been demonstrated later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's apparently been an error in translation because I didn't ask you about security.
