You said that at that time the British security service agent was there for meetings regarding protection, meetings regarding protection. My question is: What meetings regarding protection were going on on 21 May 2002? What were those meetings about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've moved dates now. You're not wanting information about 21 June 1999, which was the original question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just misspoke. It was 21 June 1999 when he was giving the interview. That's the date I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if something would have been leaked from that meeting, if -- I would be subject to persecution. Well, you know, leaks are possible, and at that time one could lose their head in Serbia because of cooperating with the ICTY. And this is still valid. Of course, I was concerned with possible leaks that would jeopardise my life, but I don't believe that there were any leaks because of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, isn't it true that what you're saying there is that at that time you were having initial meetings regarding the possibility of you going into the witness protection programme; that's what you mean, "meetings regarding protection," don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, Mr. Ackerman. At that time we did not discuss witness protection programme. We even did not discuss testimony. It was people from the investigations department who conducted some preliminary talks with me to see how I could contribute to the investigation. We did not discuss witness protection programme, protective mechanisms. I discussed with the British a situation what would happen if information were to be leaked. And at that time, and still today, one can lose their head if cooperating with the ICTY in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you testified in Milosevic on the 21st of May, 2002, for some reason Mr. Milosevic asked you about that. "Is it the position that you'll be given a new identity," this is page 5210, line 5, "a new position in another country? I don't want the details, but just whether that fact is true or not." Your answer at that time was: "That is absolutely untrue. A new identity abroad, I never discussed that with anybody, nor would I accept it. I have no reason to ask for a new identity. Protection is one matter; a new identity is another matter." That's what you said in 2002, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This refers to the initial talks with the Tribunal. Later on it transpires that the level of problem was much higher, and then I decided to accept witness protection programme and new identity. Initially I did not insist on that. You can check it with the OTP. There were no arrangements tit for tat with the OTP to the effect that they would give me a new identity in consideration for my statement. This all happened after I'd been abducted, tortured, and after it transpired that there were additional problems in Hungary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop, please. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've given your answer. Thank you. Another issue now. During your testimony here, you have taken the position that in March of 1999, as the NATO bombing came close and Rambouillet concluded, that in the Assembly right before the war that Milosevic and his associates misled the Assembly about the nature of the diplomatic situation that existed at that moment. And you said at page 6394 of your 13 November testimony: "Since he presented this as a military ultimatum, the proposal was rejected and Holbrooke went home with Serbia's decision to go into war. It was made based on wrong interpretation and wrong information, and Mr. Milutinovic participated in that because it was not correct that NATO insisted on its own flag and its own mandate. It was always under the mandate of the Security Council and the UN flag, plus the Pristina Corps, which were allowed to stay in Kosovo in the field." Now, that's your testimony, and let me just ask you if it's -- if this is not the case. At the end of Rambouillet, NATO presented a plan for ending hostilities in Kosovo which would be safe-guarded by its forces. Once the Albanian leadership had accepted it, NATO's proposal essentially became an ultimatum to Belgrade. Now, that's the truth, isn't it? That's what really happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the -- usher, can we please bring up P474, which we'll have to look at in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you're not answering my question. Could you do that, please.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I said, and I categorically repeat, that there was always a possibility for the NATO mandate to be converted into a UN Security Council mandate, and it wasn't such a big problem as presented by Milosevic, Milutinovic, and other associates. Rambouillet agreement was as it was because our delegation was not cooperative during the meeting. Had international participation been accepted during that meeting and had we said only under the UN Security Council mandate, then that would have been resolved in that way. And this is internationally verifiable. But when our side never accepted anything, never accepted the troops, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look now at the exhibit. Let's look at page 23 of the English and page 65 of the B/C/S of the document that's before you right now. And what I want you to look for is Appendix B. This is the Rambouillet agreement, the final draft, the final draft. Not a preliminary draft, as you said the other day, but this is the final draft. And if you look you'll see Appendix B on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if we can go down to paragraph 4 under there, and that's probably a page or two further along on the B/C/S version. It will be the next page no doubt. We're looking for after paragraph (H), then we'll find a number 4 on the B/C/S, please. On the B/C/S, please. We have to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English was okay, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, the English was fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now we've lost it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I think - although I don't read B/C/S - that what you see there is reference to NATO military personnel wearing uniforms, NATO personnel possessing and carrying arms; in other words, all NATO. There's nothing there about UN or UN flag. And now if we look at paragraph 8, that paragraph says, and we'll get to it here at a minute. We're at 6. We just have to go to the next page to get to 8 in the B/C/S and the English. We have it in the English. Now if we can get paragraph 8 in B/C/S we'd be there. Paragraph 8 says - there it is - "NATO personnel shall enjoy together with their vehicles, vessels, aircraft, and equipment, free and unrestricted passage and unimpeded access throughout the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, including associated air space and territorial waters. This shall include, but not be limited to, the right of bivouac, manoeuvre, billet, and utilisation of any areas or facilities as required for support, training, and operations." All NATO, no UN; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but this is the final draft. I am talking you about the options existing during the negotiations, and that option was not taken by Milosevic's regime. They didn't say, Okay, we accept the troops but under a UN flag, and that problem would have been resolved. The final draft and final agreement refers to NATO, yes, and this is what Milosevic's regime wanted. I have to answer your question. I know this final agreement. I'm aware of it. But still there was a chance - and you can verify it with Holbrooke - to say at the Assembly that we accept the troops but we don't accept NATO troops, let it be under UN Security Council's mandate. And then there was a great deal of chance to change that at the very last day, but nobody took a constructive view in the parliamentary debate. Everybody harped on the troops. Nobody said, Okay, let's be constructive and let's change the mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us all of this. And the other day what you told us when you were asked about this you said, "Well, that was the preliminary agreement not the final agreement." Now we're talking about the final agreement, and your position is that the Assembly was misled about the contents of this final agreement by people saying that it had to do with NATO troops and not UN troops. And what I'm trying to show you is that this final agreement had to do only with NATO troops, had to do only with NATO occupation of Serbia. And if you look at paragraph 21, it authorises NATO to detain persons. And then finally, if you look at chapter 8, article 1, paragraph 1 -- paragraph 3, it says that that situation will prevail for three years. So when people are telling the Assembly that this is a major surrender of sovereignty to NATO, they were telling the Assembly the truth, in spite of what you say. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did not inform them about possible options existing during negotiations and on the very last day of negotiations. Simply, they did not inform them about all the options. Of course the last and final draft refers to NATO, NATO, NATO. But I categorically maintain - and this is verifiable through much more important people in the diplomatic circles in the west than I am - that there was still possibility for the NATO flag and NATO troops to be under UN flag. Why did -- why did NATO, after winning the war, accept the UN Security Council's mandate? As a victorious party, they accepted the UN Security Council mandate. Why wouldn't they then do so before the war? I'm telling you this, and you may lead witnesses who may prove or disprove this. Well, this final draft is the result of the very hard core stance of the Milosevic regime, and Milosevic's regime's wish was to provoke a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Six times. Now, it's the case, isn't it, that the decision of the National Assembly on 23 March 1999, when boiled down to an official decision, provided that the Assembly would not accept the presence of foreign military troops in Kosovo; and provided that, upon signing of a political agreement agreed to and accepted by representatives of all national communities living in Kosovo and Metohija, the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia is ready to discuss the size and character of the international presence in Kosovo and Metohija for implementation of the agreement. Now, that was the decision, not a rejection, but an invitation to discuss international presence in Kosovo, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? Now we are interpreting things. To send such a decision after missing ten chances for an agreement and on the 11th occasion, now you want to discuss and negotiate -- well, the Americans and the Brits would say, Too little too late. There were ten missed chances before that. You can discuss this with people who are much more meritorious about this than I am, and they will confirm this. I did not take place in parliamentary or assembly debate, nor in Rambouillet. Rambouillet was too late. I am telling you an agreement was possible in 1997, and this should have been done then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Told us. And I'm trying to finish and I'm almost done. I've just got two or three questions to ask you, and I think we can get through it quickly, maybe we can. But I'm going to try. You've told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've already had 40 minutes more than anyone else. I'm sorry to have to get into this kind of situation, but you were much longer than you indicated yesterday in what you describe as not your best moment. So I wonder how necessary it all is, Mr. Ackerman. But, please, try and finish and then we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us in your testimony that you were detailed by the SDB with the consent of Milosevic during the bombing to engage in negotiations to try to find a solution to stop the bombing and to stop the war. My only question is: Why would Milosevic send you off to talk to low-level diplomats, when he could simply pick up the phone and talk to Holbrooke or Albright or Clark or anyone else to negotiate this himself? Why would he send you, someone with little skill, little ability, in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I object to the form of that question, Your Honour, little skill, little ability, where is the foundation for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll leave off that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why would he send you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That might be a question for us at the end of the day, Mr. Ackerman, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll skip that, Your Honour, because I want to finish, and I want to finish right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, your basic thesis is that you and persons you dealt with on the Albanian side worked out a settlement of the Kosovo crisis, which should have been acceptable to Milosevic, but that Milosevic really wanted war and so rejected all your efforts. Now, I suggest to you that the fundamental flaw in this thesis is that you had no contacts with the KLA, you had no agreement with the KLA for any of your proposals, and the KLA was not about to settle for anything less than full independence. And that's the situation that existed. Your negotiations with persons in the Albanian government were useless because you didn't negotiate with the KLA. You had no agreement with them. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time while we were negotiating, the KLA were a minor political force, a minor terrorist organisation. And political leaders of the Albanians in Kosovo wanted to get rid of them. Of course KLA was a threat to the normal politicians in Kosovo, such as Agani and Rugova. KLA was not included in the negotiations because the KLA was minor. Their leaders were abroad, like bouncers or body-guards at disco clubs. In 1995, 1996, 1997, Albanian terrorism did exist. It was a tragic phenomenon, but the KLA personnel were not the leading political force in Kosovo, which were -- they were converted into my Milosevic later on. They did not have any legitimacy during our negotiations. When KLA started and when Milosevic established contacts with them, we knew that this would fall through. Milosevic had two or three years to resolve the Kosovo problem after Dayton Accords. He did not do so. KLA outsmarted us and that was the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And my final question: It's your contention that the obstacle to settlement, at the time the problem existed, was the intransigence of Milosevic and his associates. Milosevic is dead. He's been out of power for seven years. Why is there still a problem?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the first part of your question, read page 239 from the book that the Defence purports to use against me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, please answer the question. Don't divert attention from the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise. Now it is a problem. It's practically an unresolvable problem for two reasons. The first reason is that Serbia lost the war with the NATO pact, which it never should have gone into it; and the second reason is that civilian natives among Kosovo Albanians gave KLA political legitimacy, which the KLA would not have received had this problem been done in peaceful and diplomatic means and not through terrorism. Now Albanian independence is a sure thing. But it wasn't down to Mil --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have something else to say that is an answer to my question? Because I don't want to cut you off, and I want to give you a fair opportunity to answer the question. So if you have something else to say, go ahead and say it.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to supplement with -- by your leave and by the Court's leave. It wasn't the problem in Milosevic, but Milosevic's belligerent policies. One of their leaders, Veton Surroi, when I told him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not answering this question, is it? You're being asked why it's still a problem, not why it was a problem when Milosevic was there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the KLA had gained political legitimacy due to such Serbian policies. Now they are running the show in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered that already. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've completed my questions and I want to express my gratitude to the Chamber for giving me the time to complete my cross-examination. And I promise you, I'll make it up to you in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Tanic, I wonder if you can briefly answer the question that Mr. Ackerman departed from, which was: Why do you think you were sent to negotiate, rather than Milosevic just directly deal with the leaders, the powerful leaders, of the west, with whom he could have reached agreement? Is there a short answer you can give us to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time whoever could establish contacts did so. I wasn't the only one doing so with regard to Milosevic. I don't know, Your Honour. He was a strange person. He never resolved matters that would be to the benefit of Serbia or himself. He was obsessed with belligerent policies, and I am flabbergasted that he did not pick up the phone. Why would Lilic go, as I learned later? I or somebody else? He could have picked up the phone and resolved that. He could have picked up the phone, and he would have pre-empted Kosovo conflict, the war with NATO. Mr. Milosevic was that kind of a person and some of his associates. When steeped in belligerent policies, they completely lose sight of self-preservation mechanisms for them and their country. I was really aghast that he would engage in such policies which ended up in tragedy for his own people, let alone other peoples. I was really flabbergasted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will resume with Mr. Lukic when we return. Could you leave now please with the usher, Mr. -- Oh, sorry, we'll go into closed session for that purpose and you can leave the courtroom. And we'll be resuming at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please wait. The blinds are producing far too strong a sound to be able to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try to put concise questions to you and I would like to hear the same answers, if I may; and the people that we cannot name will be referred to in initials as (redacted). Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the addendum you stated that your main contact was (redacted); and when decisions needed to be made, you met with Zoran Mijatovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did I understand properly that only the two, these two SDB members, that they were the only two people that you had physical contact with as regards your contacts with the SDB?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, there was some other people you had contacts with?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us their names? Or if you prefer, we may move into private session.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there is any need for it. On two occasions I was able to contact Mr. Stanisic, but I can't say that such contacts were of the working nature. I contacted some other people as well. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're going to just momentarily go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I presume I need to continue with my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had contacts with the person for whom I am uncertain of his identity as well, but this was one of the top people. It was during the war; and, unfortunately, through the beatings and the torture I underwent, I contacted with Zivaljevic, Goran Zivaljevic. He was in charge of the operation. He belonged to the service, and this is how we met. This is a contact as well, I guess, because he also had a couple of interesting things to say during the torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, these are all the people that you had contact with from the SDB. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but un -- but the focus should remain with my contacts with Mr. Mijatovic and the two aforementioned persons. These contacts were regular. They lasted for years, whereas the other contacts appeared irregularly, as far as I can recall. I hope you will not hold me to my word on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as you said, there were no working contacts with Jovica Stanisic. You had no working with contact with Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Zivaljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for Mr. Stanisic, there was a short working contact. It was very brief. We exchanged a couple of sentences. We didn't sit down and discuss matters. I used to do that with Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On how many occasions did you have contact with Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On two or three occasions, I believe. I think I mentioned that in the statement, and I don't find it to be particularly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct in saying that you were an operational contact of number 1, who was an SDB operative?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was my operational contact with Mijatovic and Stanisic, of course; so it went both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us precisely during what time did you have operational contact with number 1, in what period?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With some interruption, about two -- 20 or 25 years with interruptions, because he would go down to Kosovo and come back; and then when he was absent, number 2 was the operational contact with the top of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you cooperate with number 1 the last time, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was after he returned from Kosovo. I believe it was in 1998. It seems there were some problems subsequently, as I heard, and then number 2 was in charge of that operational contact. But please, don't hold me to it when I talk about 1998. I think it was 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did number 1 work as an operative, or did he conduct analysis?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first he was an operative, and later I believe he was promoted. And he became an analyst; however, the operational contact with me remained since we knew each other for many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The interruption of cooperation with number 1, was it preconditioned by Mijatovic leaving the service?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't link the two. My impression was -- well, I can't really explain. I think there was some problems with number 1 as far as I could hear, and then the contact was transferred to number 2. Whether it had to do with Mijatovic or something personally connected to number 1 and Kosovo, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While Jovica Stanisic was in the service, and of course Mijatovic just under him, and then further down number 1, as far as I understand there were no obstacles to having any type of contact; however, after Stanisic and Mijatovic left, did you have contact with the top of the SDB, for example, with Rade Markovic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mijatovic left after Stanisic had left. So he stayed a few months longer. My contact with Mijatovic was resumed, it went on; and once he left, for a while there was an interruption. And then when there was the NATO intervention, then the contacts were renewed via number 2, who told me that he was given a clear mandate by the top of the SDB for what we were doing. And I hope that he would confirm my words. Directly with Mr. Rade Markovic, well, I never met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When Mijatovic left, who replaced him, and did you have any contact with that person?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who replaced Mijatovic. As I said, there was an interruption, and I kept seeing number 2 on occasion, to sit down and have coffee. But our positions differed, and then our contacts were re-established once the war began; and then number 2 told me that the top of the service, irrespective of our different positions, they wanted to renew contact with me so that I could be tasked with certain duties that may contribute to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when the cooperation, the institutional cooperation, was interrupted?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to recall because it was a brief interruption. Mijatovic remained a few months after Stanisic. I think Stanisic left in November and Mijatovic stayed until new year 1998, and then in March of that year there was the war. So the interruption was brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus now on the mission we mentioned and the helicopter. It is the mission in which Stanisic participated as well, and it was in January/February 1998. Did I understand correctly that the report of that mission contained conclusions, one of them being that the reserve police force, that is the public security, was disbanded; that there were criminals among their ranks who overdid things; and that the SDB was involved in smuggling drugs. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that it is in the official report. In the official report, you cannot find that. I've heard about the mission from Mr. Perisic, just to be clear. Could you please turn off your microphone. First of all, I heard about the mission from Mr. Perisic. I heard through Stanisic for some efforts by the -- of some efforts by the service to work on things, but at that time already there were rumours that the SDB was guilty of this and that; that instead of controlling the border they were smuggling drugs. As for the police being disbanded, I don't know whether it was entered into any official documents, but I believe that was one of the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It seemed illogical to me to see that Jovica Stanisic, who headed the SDB, would write a report in which he would state that his service was involved in smuggling drugs. I believe you've responded to that, of course, by saying that such a report was never actually compiled.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I will wait for the interpretation. Of course Mr. Stanisic wouldn't put that in a report, particularly since it was incorrect. As I was told by Perisic and as far as I could hear, concerning the political exchanges that were going on, it came from Sainovic and his associates that the SDB was guilty of this and that… and also from Minic, etc… and that inter alia, they were engaged in smuggling drugs and all that. Simply, the SDB was a good target at the time concerning the situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Page 72, line 11, instead of "Stanisic," it should read "Sainovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: MR. LUKIC: [Interpretation] You talk about the commission founded by Milosevic on Monday, the 13th of November, 2006 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 72, line 11? Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Line 14, Your Honours, instead of line 11. It should read "Sainovic" instead of "Stanisic."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what the witness said, according to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you say: As I was told by Perisic and as far as could hear concerning the political exchanges that were going on, it came from," someone, "and his associates that the SDB was guilty of this and that, including smuggling drugs." Who was the person you referred to in that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was told by Perisic, but I also heard that from Mihajlovic and Mijatovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, who did Perisic refer to? Somebody and his associates. Who was the somebody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me and the other people did, too, but this is within a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For some reason you're not following this. You said: "As I was told by Perisic and as far as I could hear, it came from," and there's a name there, "and his associates that the SDB was guilty of smuggling drugs." Now, who was the person that was referred to there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation was not completely correct, but I had Mijatovic in mind as someone who told me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic says you said, "Sainovic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. Yes, that's correct. I did mention. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in line 11 I saw name Stanisic not Sainovic. You referred to line 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, line 14 you said. Line 11 was the one initially you sought to change and then you corrected that to line 14. Do you want to change line 11 or line 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't say this. I didn't say this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was an interpreter's correction, Your Honour, not Mr. Lukic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that moment witness said "Stanisic" and it was 11 -- line 11 was "Stanisic." You pointed line 11, and I confirm that it should be Stanisic in line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, look at page 72, line 17. You sought to correct line 11. And when I went to deal with that you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't say this. I think that it was or your line or -- but this is not my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. The question, page 72, line 11, instead of "Stanisic," it should read "Sainovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what happened is the interpreter indicated that they had incorrectly interpreted what Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, start again, Mr. Lukic. I'm not going back over this. If you want the answer clarified, you need to get it from the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask for this clarification at all, Your Honour, so I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tanic, I just asked you about the 13th of November, 2006, on this trial that you stated that the state commission was established towards the end of 1997 or the end of 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my memory, it is correct. Maybe my memory plays tricks on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you tell -- who told you about the establishment of this commission?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was discussed in Belgrade among political and intelligence circles. I spoke to seven, eight, or five, six, maybe eight, nine persons about that. I cannot pin-point who told me that, whether I heard it from Mihajlovic or through my intelligence contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 82 of your statement you say that: "Most of my information on the work of the state commission comes from Perisic."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing is to establish a commission; operation is quite another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do agree. Was Perisic member of that state commission?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not meddle with military police and intelligence composition of that commission. I was entered in the political side of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Perisic member of that commission, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you - and I'll give you reference in the transcript, 6383, paragraph 86 of your statement and 6383 from the transcript. It concerns a telephone conversation that you mentioned between Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Lukic. And you were questioned by my colleague Fila about that. Unfortunately, I will have to re-visit this issue. First of all, I would like to ask you about the facts. In your statement, your original statement, you said: "From my Western sources, it was confirmed that there were at least one taped conversation." In supplementary information that we received from the OTP concerning your proofing on the 5th of November, 2006, you correct that and now we have before us an information whereby you say: "My Western sources and from the SDB confirmed this taped conversation between Sainovic and Lukic from early 1999." Later on we established - and as you claim - that information really came both from the west and from the SDB, and you later stated that you heard this conversation. What happened before and what after? Did you first receive information from the west, or did you receive information from the SDB? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very slippery slope. I believe that the first the information came from the west, but I think so. Let it be reflected in the transcript that is my opinion. I didn't say that I listened to the whole tape. I just heard it. Whether it was a part of the tape or the whole tape, I really cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you: How did it transpire that in the statement that you gave on several occasions -- on seven occasions did you speak to the OTP and you provided specific information about this case, but in none of the seven occasions that you had conversation with the OTP you mentioned this, that you personally heard that tape and you failed to mention that you received that information from the SDB. Do you have an explanation for this, please?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have great problems with this tape because I heard it under circumstances which are extremely unusual, and I could not verify that tape. And this is why, most probably, I did not mention it. I've heard and seen many things throughout the years that I could not verify, and I failed to mention those things that I could not verify in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not mention this in Milosevic's trial either in the way that you mentioned it in November this year. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I just mentioned to the OTP that I heard it, but I never really dwelled on it. If I were to try to reproduce everything I heard or saw, then this would resemble a science fiction story, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although you already stated that you could not, but is it true that you cannot tell us this western source who gave you this information?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you, but I may supplement my earlier answer and what jogged my memory and prompted me to mention this tape --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. We've moved on to this issue of the western source. What did you hear from that western source about the date when this tape was taken, recorded?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not enter into that because there are many tapes, many recordings. I dislike tapes, electronic surveillance, wire-tapping. I'm not an expert in that anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there anybody else --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Lukic. You were going to say something else about what had jogged your memory. Could you tell us what that was, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simply, it slipped my mind. It is not true that this tape was not referred to in Milosevic's trial. Now I remember that I did mention it. It slipped my mind that this tape or parts of that tape were publicly disclosed. But I don't know who gave what to whom. At any rate, after a while, after hearing parts or the whole tape, I could hear something similar or read in one of the Belgrade media outlets, and this gave me a jolt, so to speak. And since it referred Racak, I did mention this tape in Milosevic's trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. You did mention the tape but you didn't mention that you heard it, and you received it from the SDB as an information. You still refer to it as an information received from western sources.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge May rejected that, because he characterised that as a public source after it had been published and not something that I learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, then could you tell us whether on the Milosevic trial it was said and proven where that tape was published so that we can really try to find it, please.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bench did not enter into this, Mr. May's Bench, because the tape was mentioned in relation to with Racak. And since this was a public source, as far as I can remember, he rejected any discussion about that. Let's take a look at the notes or the transcript, and now may I answer the question of His Honour. By sorting out my memories in preparation for this trial, I remembered that it was published somewhere; and then having realised that I tried to say, Let's sort this thing out, try to see where it was published. Because I'm not testifying here to sling mud, but to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you -- have we clarified this thing? Did you find where it was published, please?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was on B92. The translation is incorrect. I said I believe it was B92. It should state, I think it was 92. It could be something else altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You think, but you never personally heard this on B92. Is that correct, or not?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the transcript in the papers or in the press-clipping published by B92. And I thought to myself, What's this? This is something that I had occasion to hear previously. Could you switch your mikes off while I'm talking? My microphone is not -- there's a feedback. Now it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You do not remember where -- when was it that you read it on B92 site, or do you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I cannot be very precise about it, and I don't want this lacuna in my memory to bring about more aggro.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Was anybody else present on the moment when you received that information from a western source?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We personally spoke, the two of us, about the parallel chain of command which is something which was discussed, and western source said that there were certain recordings. And we did not explore that further. I'm not an expert in wire-tapping. I never dealt with that, and I don't put much store in it. I was wire-tapped on several occasions, and these tapes did not prove to be of much use for those who were taping them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's just stick to the questions, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, let us move on. Do you know when did this conversation between Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Lukic did take place, the one that we are referring to here?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could hear, the conversation concerned Racak [Realtime transcript read in error "Vracar"]. Let's try to remind ourselves when -- no, it's not "Vracar."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. It's going to be corrected in the transcript. I meant Racak. When did you hear this conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's -- let's stop --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You may use your notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's stop again. I'm sorry I don't have an override button for this type of evidence, that's why I have to raise my voice to try and interrupt. It says there: "No. It's going to be corrected in the transcript. I meant Racak." Now, was that not part of the answer? It's labelled as a question, but is that not part of the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. It was my, actually, question. I said it would be corrected because the witness meant Racak not Vracar. Because he intervened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So can we go back - and you may consult your notes if you have them with you. Could you remember when did you hear this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any notes with me. As far as I can remember, it was immediately before -- no, between my two trips during wartime, as far as my memory serves me. So much later than Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, could you tell us who enabled you to hear this conversation? ?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already stated, I cannot name that person for several reasons. I can state my reasons again in public session. That person may feel threatened. They may be really threatened. My answer would be negative. Another reason: I cannot verify it. I did not tape that conversation. I was not part of that tape being produced. I cannot verify the voices --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on because of lack of time. So it's neither number 1 nor number 2, neither Jovica Stanisic, nor Mijatovic, none of those persons?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So if you were -- so the person that you had not cooperated previously made it possible for you to hear that tape, is it true or not?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can -- you can't put it this way that we had not cooperated. I cooperated with the top brass of both services, with one echelon in peacetime and with other people in wartime. But I don't have personal knowledge about that person. I don't know him. I hadn't worked with him. The circumstances were such that -- that there was no doubt as to whether he was a high official in the service or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how come that a person with whom you had not cooperated would made -- make you privy to information that may jeopardise him if it were correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know very well the intelligence community. There were ploys, counter-ploys, information, misinformation. That person knew who I was. I'm not an unknown person to the intelligence apparatus. Maybe they wanted to do something else with that tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could it be possible that that person wanted to play a trick on you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? Since I have some indications that that person was involved in the kidnapping of me and my wife, the torture and the attempted murder of me and my wife, I had now reason to believe that that person wanted me, at the time, to know something; and maybe later on that person was repentant. And this is why I was -- I had reservations about that tape. But why I believe it, because it conforms to some other information obtained from some other forces when it came to excessive use of force in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us in what building on what address did you hear this tape?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to explain that in private session, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll go into private session to hear this to protect the identity of the individual involved.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The SDB employee, did he have to ask for authorisation from his superiors to as to be able to share that information with you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it was wartime. There were special police members and JSO members among his security. I don't think he asked for anything; but at that time of course, I cannot fully reconstruct the processes and methods used because it involved people I didn't know. These were no longer Mijatovic and Stanisic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sometimes both His Honour and myself may appear rough, but we are pressed with time. And there is a real danger of not finishing today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this has got to the stage where I would interrupt these, even if we had appear eternity to take the evidence because the witness is constantly not confining himself to the questions that are asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree, but I'm trying to soothe it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tanic, did you listen to any other previously intercepted conversations; and if so, could you tell us where, with whom, and what conversations?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never listened to such tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic's microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have to repeat, since my microphone was off. After that, did you ever listen to any intercepts; and if so, when, with whom, and who was involved?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was only able to listen to my own intercepts of my own conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which media was used? Was it a tape-player, a computer, a CD player?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tape was transferred. That's why I believe I only listened to parts of it. It was transferred to a regular tape. That's why I thought it was not the original tape, because they probably look different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us conclude on this topic, since we are unable to hear from you who gave you that opportunity to listen. You also told us that you didn't listen to the entire conversation. You didn't hear the beginning of it when the two collocutors introduced themselves. You didn't recognise the voices of Mr. Lukic and Mr. Sainovic. And am I correct in saying that you learned about the identity of people involved from someone else. Someone else told you who the people were?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Now you understand why I -- why I had reservations about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please focus on paragraph 102 of your statement, the incident in Prekaze. In the transcript, it is page 6372. When talking about the operation in Prekaze you say that in early 1998, you learned via your SDB contacts about the operation -- of the operation. Can you tell us who provided that information to you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Mr. Mijatovic. He conveyed that information to me. He said that because of two terrorists, half of the village was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you learn of this operation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise as to the date. It was immediately after ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You learned that from Mr. Mijatovic. Was he there on the spot during the operation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose an operative must have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in the course of this trial we saw some photographs gained from foreign sources, in which we can see that not only -- not only that the village was [as interpreted] destroyed, but even the Jashari house was fairly intact. Therefore, the information you received that half of the village was destroyed, would you accept that it was not correct? I mean the operation when the Jasharis were attacked and when an attempt to arrest them was made.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was colloquially speaking that half of the village was destroyed. No one really meant it. I wasn't down there, and I never said I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that the question was: Not only that the village was not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was just warned by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tanic, according to an OTP statement of a witness, the pseudonym of whom is K64 and he's yet to testify, did you know that the operation was headed by Jovica Stanisic himself?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I clearly stated that this was not my direct knowledge. As to whether Mr. Stanisic was in charge of the operation, I don't know. I received the information I shared with you, and I conveyed it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To move on to the Decani incident, which took place after the Prekaze incident, and you mentioned that in paragraph 97. It is mentioned in the transcript at page 6360. There you state in April 1998 in Decani, the reserve police forces were sent there as well as paramilitary forces and a brigade of the VJ. You said you were told that by number 1. When did you hear that from him?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shortly afterwards. He returned from Kosovo. He was on short leave. We met, so it must have been shortly afterwards. He said he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he say that this operation was headed by Jovica Stanisic as well?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that. He didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that on that occasion it didn't concern the neutralisation of several snipers, but rather to lift the blockade of the Pec-Djakovica road, including the obstacle set at Decani, because that communication was under KLA control at the time? Did anyone tell you that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mentioned the snipers. But since I took no part in the combat down there and I wasn't much interested in it, that's how I took the information he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 103 you say: "The special police behaviour and the anti-terrorist unit's behaviour, as well as the security units and combined military and police units and the JSO, their behaviour and their conduct is regulated by rules of service." Can you tell us which rules of service regulate that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules of service of the Ministry of the Interior on the use of such units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The whole of the MUP? The rules pertaining to the State Security Service or the public security service?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise as to that. I think it is the rules of service of the MUP, but I really cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do the rules regulate the use of combined military/police units?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be regulated that way, and I don't think the translation in the statement was correct since the JSO was not a special police of the -- unit of the police, but rather of the State Security Service. They were commanded by the SDB. Military police units and then the JSO in the same paragraph, it doesn't quite tally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, that part of the statement is incorrect. Let us move on then. Paragraph 103, you state --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic should be warned to read slowly when reading texts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're being asked when you're reading to read more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to backtrack a little. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 103 you state: "The rules of service, or rather, the rules of procedure are considered to be a state secret." Which rules of procedure did you have in mind in this case?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules of procedure on use of special forces of the MUP and the rules of engagement when combatting terrorism. These are the rules of procedure of the MUP. You're asking me to recollect things in which I'm not expert. I cannot be as specific as I can be when talking about intelligence and politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you see these rules of procedure?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in government, while we were part of the coalition, at a certain point I was able to read a few things regarding the use of special forces. It was a photocopy that I read, and first and foremost I mentioned that in the context of distinguishing between civilians and terrorists. That's why I was interested in it. I wasn't much interested in the rules of procedure of use of special units. It is not within my scope of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who made it possible for you to see these rules, because they are a state secret?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. You're asking me about things which were of tangential nature. This was based on the experience of other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... At the moment. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also state -- well, do you remember what the book looked like, the book containing the rules? What colour was it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I was given a photocopy of certain pages. I -- it was not a thick book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore you didn't see the whole book?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also say that special forces had to abide by these rules in paragraph 104 of your statement. Otherwise, for any infractions one can be given a jail sentence of up to ten years. Which law foresees this prison sentence of ten years, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. That information is something that I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Then next you say: "Our law is quite strict on it, although it is not in the rules of procedure in exceptional cases when a commander has lost control and endangers his unit, he may even be executed by his colleagues and superiors."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic should be reminded to read slowly for the interpreters to be able to locate the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that information came from? Is that in any piece of legislation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding gained through my conversations with several people when it comes to combat activities, conditions, and the threatening of lives -- or risk the lives of one's own men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who told you that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. One of the SDB people with whom I cooperated. I clearly said that there is a possibility of being executed; I didn't say that there will be executions. This was simply an impression I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You also described in paragraph 105 rules of procedure and the procedure whereby anti-terrorist units should act. In these rules that you saw, does it really stand that when terrorists are targeted and when special units act against terrorists, that they are bound to fire in the air a warning shot, that they should use gas, rubber bullets? Did it really stand in the rules that you purport to have read? ?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't stand in the rules, but these were applied as far as I could understand. I understood that civilians should be separated from terrorists by some means, use of rubber bullets, warning shots. This is something which was not prescribed by rules, but mechanisms of separating civilians from terrorists. That was in the rules. I used those rules just once and it's very awkward for me to have to answer questions about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do understand that. But in paragraph 105 of your statement it says that these rules prescribe and a reader may gain an impression that this is prescribed by such rules. Now we can agree that this is not what the rules prescribe, then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot recollect. I believe that these rules prescribe this or that, but I'm not sure -- I'm certain that they do not prescribe the exact technical means, rubber bullets, tear gas, et cetera. But I -- this is my recollection of these rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When terrorists intervene in a plane full of civilians then such measures would be used. Would we agree that they would have no obligation to separate the civilians from the terrorists because this is impossible and in such situations it is presumed that there civilian casualties, but the terrorists are to blame and not the special police units that are intervening. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conviction is that what happened down on the ground in Kosovo is not the same as a plane full of civilians. My belief is that civilians can be separated primarily by waiting for the terrorists to be exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another thing I'd like to ask you is as we saw you were abducted by members of the JSO, and that's a unit under the purview of the sector of state security. Is that correct? Let's not bicker about whether it was an arrest, a kidnapping, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tanic. I have no further questions for you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I need five minutes, maybe less.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tanic, my name is Mihajlo Bakrac, counsel -- one of the counsel for General Lazarevic. I have practically one question. During your examination-in-chief and during cross-examination and just now, you spoke about the alleged state commission and you were asked about its membership. Is it true that previously you stated that General Lazarevic was not a member of the state commission?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I cannot recall now because I was interested in the political part of those affairs. I cannot recall whether I stated that Lazarevic was or was not a member. I cannot recall. I never dealt with the full membership of that commission whenever I was discussing that with the Prosecution, because I always maintained that I am not an expert in military and police affairs, just the political dimension of this affair and intelligence dimension of the political dimension of the affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: May I -- if it will jog your memory, I will read to -- your statement from 1998/1999. "Lazarevic did not have a complete picture of what was going on because he was not a member of that commission." Do you recall now? This is paragraph 86.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably I stated that because it was written down. I cannot say that I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, I do not have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in a difficult position. This witness was scheduled to fly on an early-morning flight. I don't think I can get him done in the remaining ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I know the Court suggested that they may have questions after you've heard all the examination. If that's true, what I would propose is -- is if we have to keep him here to finish him, I would rather stop now and be more focused tomorrow morning than to try and do ten minutes now when I'm not going to get him completed anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, my note at the moment is there were two matters -- two identities that the witness refused to give and explained why. One was the person who gave access to the tape that's been the subject of recent cross-examination, and the other was the person who told him to go abroad during the war for discussions. Was there any other issue left outstanding in your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The thing is that I wanted to obtain names of persons so that I could conduct my investigation to see whether this was as explained or not. No other. I believe that he named an insufficient number of people, and that is all for me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I take it you wish to press both of these, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I told the Court that I proceeded as far as I could, and then it was up to you to take the torch on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Tanic, was the person who told you to go abroad during the war for the discussions you had, the same person as the person who gave you access to the Sainovic-Lukic conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there are two persons involved. Now, Mr. Ackerman, is there an identity that you still seek to obtain?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, only the -- the NATO diplomat, and I think you know the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, we would welcome some guidance as far as you can give it, and you can do that tomorrow also, in relation to these three issues. Because depending on the importance, it may not simply be a question of weight. There can be circumstances in which we would have to leave out of account the evidence surrounding the subject matter that these various issues arise in. And we may take a different view in relation to each one. But the first decision we have to take is whether to insist on the witness's -- the personnel being identified. And on that, I think you will be able to give us some more guidance, having reflected on it overnight and having had a chance to look at your position in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we'll adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00. We need to go into closed session for the witness to leave. I'm afraid your return to your home will be delayed, Mr. Tanic. You will require to return tomorrow for your evidence to be completed; that will be at 9.00 tomorrow. Meanwhile, no discussion, again, with anyone about your evidence, even though you're so far through it, it's even more important now that there should be no such discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 17th day of November, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.42 p.m.,
